title: A tiny health check
prompt: Implement healthCode() to return the integer 200. The test harness supplies main(); your file only needs the function.
hints: Declare an int return type and use a return statement.
explanation: C++ needs a declared return type. The compiler turns this function into native code before it can run.

title: Count the pages
prompt: Implement pageCount(items, perPage) for nonnegative item counts and positive page sizes. Include a partially filled final page. Inputs are at most 10,000.
hints: Integer division discards the remainder. Add one page if the remainder is nonzero.
explanation: Both operands being int means division produces an int. The % operator lets you detect the leftover items.
starter: int pageCount(int items, int perPage) { return 0; }
solution: int pageCount(int items, int perPage) { return items / perPage + (items % perPage != 0); }

title: Initialize the retry budget
prompt: Inside retryBudget(), declare an int named retries, value-initialize it with {}, then add 3 and return it. Why would int retries; be unsafe here?
hints: Empty braces initialize an int to zero.
explanation: An uninitialized automatic int has no usable starting value. Unlike an absent JS value, reading it is not a predictable undefined value you can branch on.
solution: int retryBudget() { int retries{}; retries += 3; return retries; }

title: Keep the fractional seconds
prompt: Implement seconds(milliseconds) returning double. Preserve the fraction: 1250 ms is 1.25 seconds. Inputs are nonnegative.
hints: Convert before dividing, or use a floating-point divisor.
explanation: Converting an already-truncated integer result to double cannot restore the fraction. Operand types determine how the expression is evaluated.

title: A copy of the counter
prompt: Implement bumped(int counter) returning counter + 1. In a separate scratch program, call it with a local variable and verify the original is unchanged.
hints: The parameter is a separate int object initialized from the argument.
explanation: Passing an int by value copies the value. Changing the parameter does not assign to the caller’s variable.

title: A compile-time upload limit
prompt: Define constexpr int maxUploadKiB as 2048. Implement fitsUpload(int kib) for the inclusive range 0..maxUploadKiB. Explain why constexpr is stronger than const.
hints: A constexpr variable must have a constant-expression initializer.
explanation: const prevents mutation through that variable. constexpr also requires a value usable at compile time. JS const does not impose this compile-time requirement.
starter:
// TODO: maxUploadKiB
bool fitsUpload(int kib) { return false; }
solution:
constexpr int maxUploadKiB{2048};
bool fitsUpload(int kib) { return kib >= 0 && kib <= maxUploadKiB; }

title: Build a route
prompt: Implement route(std::string name) returning /api/ followed by name. Empty name should return /api/. Include the header you use.
hints: Use a std::string for the prefix; + concatenates strings.
explanation: std::string owns its characters and can grow. A string literal is not itself a std::string object.
solution:
#include <string>
std::string route(std::string name) { return std::string{"/api/"} + name; }

title: An access rule
prompt: Implement canPublish(isAdmin, isOwner, isLocked): an admin or owner may publish, but nobody may publish a locked item.
hints: Group the admin-or-owner condition before combining it with the lock check.
explanation: Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. && binds more tightly than ||, which can make an ungrouped rule accidentally allow admins through the lock.
starter: bool canPublish(bool isAdmin, bool isOwner, bool isLocked) { return false; }
solution: bool canPublish(bool isAdmin, bool isOwner, bool isLocked) { return (isAdmin || isOwner) && !isLocked; }
tests: for (bool a : {false,true}) for (bool o : {false,true}) for (bool l : {false,true}) assert(canPublish(a,o,l) == ((a || o) && !l));

title: Avoid a shadowed result
prompt: Fix status(bool ok) so it returns 200 on success and 503 otherwise. The inner declaration currently hides the outer variable.
hints: Assign to the existing result instead of declaring another int.
explanation: A nested declaration can reuse a name while referring to a different object. Updating that inner object does not change the outer one.
starter: int status(bool ok) { int result{503}; if (ok) { int result{200}; } return result; }
solution: int status(bool ok) { int result{503}; if (ok) { result = 200; } return result; }

title: Two timeout policies
prompt: Define timeout() in namespaces api and worker. Return 30 from api::timeout() and 120 from worker::timeout().
hints: Put each function inside namespace name { ... }.
explanation: Namespaces distinguish otherwise identical names. Use :: to select a namespace member; this is not object property access.
starter: // TODO: two namespaces and their timeout functions
solution:
namespace api { int timeout() { return 30; } }
namespace worker { int timeout() { return 120; } }

title: Classify a response
prompt: Implement category(int code): return 2 for 200 or 201, 4 for 400 or 404, and 0 otherwise. Practise using switch.
hints: Several case labels can share the same return statement.
explanation: A return exits the function, so these cases need no break. Without return or break, control continues into the next case.
solution: int category(int code) { switch(code) { case 200: case 201: return 2; case 400: case 404: return 4; default: return 0; } }

title: Total the retry delays
prompt: Implement totalDelay(int attempts): delays are 1, 2, ..., attempts seconds. Return their sum using a loop. attempts is in 0..100.
hints: Initialize an accumulator to zero, and include the final attempt.
explanation: A loop condition is evaluated before each iteration. For zero attempts, the body should not execute.
solution: int totalDelay(int attempts) { int total{}; for(int i{1}; i <= attempts; ++i) total += i; return total; }

title: Guard a bounded value
prompt: Implement clampPercent(int value), clamping integers to 0..100. Add your own assertions for values just inside and outside both boundaries.
hints: Check below zero first, then above 100, otherwise keep the original value.
explanation: Boundary tests distinguish < from <= mistakes and catch accidental changes to valid input. Assertions test assumptions; they are not a substitute for validating user input.
solution: int clampPercent(int value) { if(value < 0) return 0; if(value > 100) return 100; return value; }
tests: assert(clampPercent(-1)==0); assert(clampPercent(0)==0); assert(clampPercent(1)==1); assert(clampPercent(99)==99); assert(clampPercent(100)==100); assert(clampPercent(101)==100);

title: Compute a success ratio
prompt: Implement ratio(int success, int total), returning double. Return 0.0 when total is zero; otherwise return the fractional quotient. Inputs satisfy 0 <= success <= total.
hints: Guard zero, then cast an operand before division.
explanation: Casts make a conversion explicit. A double return type alone does not make an integer division floating-point.
starter: double ratio(int success, int total) { return 0.0; }
solution: double ratio(int success, int total) { if(total == 0) return 0.0; return static_cast<double>(success) / total; }

title: What does auto deduce?
prompt: Define auto batchSize initialized from 16 and auto retrySeconds initialized from 0.5. Implement auto nextBatch() to return batchSize + 1. Predict each deduced type before checking.
hints: auto deduces from the initializer expression, not future assignments.
explanation: These types are fixed at compile time. auto is type inference, not a dynamically typed container.

title: One name, two payload types
prompt: Define payloadSize(int) returning sizeof(int) as an int, and payloadSize(std::string) returning the string length as an int. Include <string>. Test both overloads.
hints: The parameter types must differ; changing only the return type cannot create an overload.
explanation: C++ overloads are distinct function implementations selected from the argument types. This differs from TypeScript overload signatures backed by a single implementation.

title: Resolve the numeric overload
prompt: Define pick(int) returning 1 and pick(double) returning 2. Implement pickHalf() calling pick with 0.5. Predict what pick(1.0f) selects.
hints: float promotes to double; an exact match beats a conversion.
explanation: The compiler ranks viable overloads. An explicit cast can make your intended argument type clear when a call would otherwise be ambiguous.

title: A default retry allowance
prompt: Implement retryWindow(int delay, int attempts = 3), returning delay * attempts. Inputs are nonnegative and at most 100. Call it with one and two arguments.
hints: Place the default on the trailing parameter.
explanation: A missing argument is supplied from the default at the call site. Adding a one-parameter overload as well would make one-argument calls ambiguous here.
solution: int retryWindow(int delay, int attempts = 3) { return delay * attempts; }
